d: Powers of two, data units, and doing big multiplications in your head
goal: Your win today: you can say '2 to the 30 is about a billion, so a gigabyte', multiply '300 million users times 1 KB' in your head (300 GB), and you never write a number on the whiteboard without its unit.
bookSections: Chapter 2 intro (Jeff Dean's definition of back-of-the-envelope estimation), 'Power of two' (Table 2-1), and the 'Tips' section items on rounding/approximation and labeling units

stages.title: Climb the byte ladder
stages.sub: Five rungs that cover every estimate you'll ever do
stages.teaches: Opening idea (book, quoting Jeff Dean, Google Senior Fellow): back-of-the-envelope calculations are estimates you build from thought experiments plus common performance numbers, to get a feel for which designs will meet your requirements. Interviewers use them to see whether you can reason about scale; precision is not the point. Data volume can get huge but the arithmetic is simple once you know the units. A byte is 8 bits. One ASCII character (plain English letter, digit, punctuation) takes 1 byte. Table 2-1: 2^10 ≈ 1 thousand = 1 KB (kilobyte); 2^20 ≈ 1 million = 1 MB (megabyte); 2^30 ≈ 1 billion = 1 GB (gigabyte); 2^40 ≈ 1 trillion = 1 TB (terabyte); 2^50 ≈ 1 quadrillion = 1 PB (petabyte). Pattern: every +10 in the exponent = ×~1000 = next unit = 3 more zeros.
stages.interaction: A vertical ladder with five empty rungs labeled 2^10, 2^20, 2^30, 2^40, 2^50 (bottom to top). Below it, two shuffled trays of chips: word chips (thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion) and unit chips (KB, MB, GB, TB, PB). Learner taps a chip, then taps a rung to place it (tap-to-place, works on mobile). A rung lights up green and shows '≈ 10^3', '≈ 10^6'… when both its chips are right; wrong placements shake and bounce the chip back (no heart cost here, practice). When all 10 chips are placed, an animated '×1000' arrow appears between each rung and a byte counter at the top rolls from 1 KB up to 1 PB. A small side card shows 'A = 1 byte (ASCII), 1 byte = 8 bits'.
stages.check: Q.quiz: '2^30 bytes is about…' options: '1 billion bytes, which is 1 GB' (correct) / '1 million bytes, which is 1 MB' / '1 trillion bytes, which is 1 TB'. Good: 'Every +10 on the exponent is ×1000 and one unit up: 10→KB, 20→MB, 30→GB.'

stages.title: The 2.4% white lie
stages.sub: Why 1024 ≈ 1000 is fine, and where it starts to drift
stages.teaches: 2^10 is really 1,024, not 1,000, so the ladder is an approximation: the error is 2.4% at KB, 4.9% at MB, 7.4% at GB, 10.0% at TB, 12.6% at PB. For an estimate that's off by at most ~13%, which is well inside 'right order of magnitude'. Real-world wrinkle: the IEC binary units KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB (kibibyte etc.) mean exact powers of two; KB/MB/GB officially mean powers of ten. Disk makers sell decimal TB, operating systems often report binary units, so a '1 TB' drive shows up as about 931 'GB' (really GiB). In an interview, say 'I'll treat 2^10 as 1,000' and move on.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch. First the learner predicts: 'How far off is 2^40 from 10^12 (one trillion)?' options 0.1% / 2.4% / 10% / 50%. Then a 'drift meter': a horizontal slider with stops at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. At each stop two bars render side by side: exact 2^n (e.g. 1,099,511,627,776) vs the round 10^(3k) (1,000,000,000,000), and a gauge shows the gap % (2.4, 4.9, 7.4, 10.0, 12.6). A gauge band from 0–25% is shaded green and labeled 'fine for napkin math'. Then a mini card: a '1 TB' drive icon; learner taps 'What does the OS show?' and it animates 1,000,000,000,000 ÷ 1024³ = 931 GiB.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: 10%). Then Q.quiz: 'Your interviewer says 2^40 is 1.1 trillion, not 1 trillion. Best reply?' options: 'True, about 10% off; fine at this level of estimate' (correct) / 'Then I need to redo every number exactly' / 'No, 2^40 is exactly one trillion bytes'.

stages.title: Count the zeros
stages.teaches: The trick: rewrite each number as (small number) × 10^k, multiply the small numbers, add the exponents, then map the exponent back to a unit (3→K, 6→M, 9→G, 12→T, 15→P). Example: 300 million users × 1 KB = 3×10^8 × 10^3 bytes = 3×10^11 bytes = 300 GB. 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB = 1.5×10^8 × 2 × 0.1 × 10^6 = 3×10^13 bytes = 30 TB (the exact Twitter media number from Quest 2.4). Percentages are just ×0.1, ×0.5 etc.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check, 4 cards in sequence. Each card shows a problem and a 'zero tally' helper: each factor appears as a chip with its mantissa and exponent (e.g. '3 × 10^8', '1 × 10^3 B'); the learner can tap a chip to see its exponent highlighted. Answer box = number field + unit dropdown (B, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB). Problems: (1) 300 million users × 1 KB profile → 300 GB; (2) 2 billion photos × 500 KB → 1 PB (1,000 TB accepted); (3) 10 million users × 2 KB → 20 GB; (4) 150 million × 2 tweets × 10% × 1 MB → 30 TB. Grading accepts any value/unit pair equivalent within ±10% (so '0.3 TB' passes for 300 GB). On a wrong answer it animates the worked line: mantissas multiply on the left, exponents add on the right, then the exponent snaps to its unit on the ladder from stage 1.
stages.check: Each card awards XP on first try; after the 4 cards, Q.quiz: '50 million users × 200 bytes of text each is about…' options '10 GB' (correct) / '10 TB' / '10 MB'.

stages.title: Round like a pro
stages.sub: The book's tips: approximate, and label every unit
stages.teaches: Book tip 1, rounding and approximation: doing 99987 / 9.1 by hand wastes interview time; round to 100,000 / 10 = 10,000. Precision is not expected. Book tip 2, label your units: writing '5' on the board is ambiguous; is it 5 KB or 5 MB? You will confuse yourself. Write 5 MB. Bonus handy constant (not in the book, but standard): a day has 86,400 seconds ≈ 10^5, so 1 million events per day ≈ 10 per second (exactly 11.6), and 1 billion per day ≈ 10,000 per second (exactly 11,574).
stages.interaction: Two mini-games. (A) Rounding sprint: 5 ugly expressions appear one at a time (99,987 / 9.1; 86,400 × 3; 1,000,000 / 86,400; 47 × 2,100; 3.65 × 300). For each, the learner first picks the best rounded form from 3 options (e.g. '100,000 / 10', '99,990 / 9', '99,987 / 9'), then the answer appears with exact vs rounded side by side and the % gap. A small stopwatch shows how long they took (no penalty; it just shows that rounding is fast). (B) Spot the unit bug: a whiteboard image with 5 lines of an estimate, e.g. 'DAU = 150 million', 'Tweet size = 1', 'Media/day = 30 TB', 'QPS ≈ 3500', 'Storage/5 yrs = 55'. Learner taps every line missing a unit (correct: 'Tweet size = 1' and 'Storage/5 yrs = 55'; QPS is fine because the unit is in its name). Tapped lines get a red underline and a tooltip suggesting the fix ('1 MB', '55 PB').
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Why does the book say to label units?' options: 'So you don't mix up 5 KB and 5 MB halfway through the math' (correct) / 'Interviewers grade you on SI notation style' / 'Units make the numbers more precise'.

stages.title: Boss: The Unit Gremlin
stages.sub: Grade the whiteboard before the interviewer does
stages.teaches: Applies stages 1–4: unit ladder, zero counting, rounding, labeling. The common bugs are off-by-1000 (one rung slipped), missing units, and fake precision.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with shared choices: '✅ Looks right', '🔢 Off by about 1000×', '📏 Unit missing', '🎯 Fake precision, round it'. Scenarios (each a whiteboard line): (1) '1 million users × 1 KB = 1 GB' → Looks right; (2) '2^40 bytes ≈ 1 PB' → Off by 1000× (it's 1 TB); (3) 'Write QPS = 3,472.2222' → Fake precision (say ~3,500); (4) 'Daily media storage: 30' → Unit missing (30 TB); (5) '5 million users × 2 MB = 10 GB' → Off by 1000× (it's 10 TB); (6) '1 billion ASCII characters ≈ 1 GB' → Looks right (1 byte each); (7) 'Peak QPS = 6,944.44 per second' → Fake precision. Each 'why' shows the corrected line.
stages.check: Boss HP bar; a wrong pick costs a heart in a first run (engine default).

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Recall of the whole quest in the learner's own words.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'The interviewer says: you have 300 million users and each profile is about 1 KB. How much storage, and how did you get there so fast?' Model answer: '300 million is 3 × 10^8, 1 KB is 10^3 bytes, add the exponents: 3 × 10^11 bytes, which is 300 GB. I'm treating 2^10 as 1,000; that's about 2.4% off per step, around 10% by terabytes, which is fine for an estimate. I'll write it as 300 GB with the unit, and round as I go, because precision isn't the point.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Converted to powers of ten and added exponents', 'Got 300 GB (with the unit)', 'Said 2^10 ≈ 1,000 and that the error is small', 'Mentioned rounding / precision not expected'.

caveats: 2^10 = 1,024, not 1,000: the ladder drifts by 2.4% per rung (about 10% at TB, 12.6% at PB). Fine for estimates, wrong for billing or capacity contracts.
Strictly, KB/MB/GB are decimal (10^3, 10^6, 10^9) and KiB/MiB/GiB are binary (2^10…). The book blurs them, as most engineers do in conversation.
'1 ASCII character = 1 byte' holds for English text; real text is UTF-8, where non-Latin characters take 2–4 bytes and emoji take 4.
The 86,400 ≈ 10^5 shortcut is not in the book; it underestimates rates by about 14%, which is why the book's Twitter example says ~3,500 QPS while the shortcut gives ~3,000.
